papers.conclusion: Learning a well-organized internal representation is a prerequisite for effective policy learning, and using pre-learned latent representations can remove this burden, leading to accelerated training.
papers.key_findings:
Agents trained on latent representations learn significantly faster than those trained on raw pixel images.
The internal representation of policies using latent codes is organized around task rewards even before training begins.
A poor initial representation (e.g., raw pixels in a complex task) can cause an unrecoverable collapse in the policy network's internal representation.
The organization of the internal representation evolves during training and correlates with learning progress.
The innate organization provided by latent representations is robust to different weight initialization schemes.
papers.abstract: We analyze the hidden activations of neural network policies of deep reinforcement learning (RL) agents and show, empirically, that it's possible to know a priori if a state representation will lend itself to fast learning. RL agents in high-dimensional states have two main learning burdens: (1) to learn an action-selection policy and (2) to learn to discern between useful and non-useful information in a given state. By learning a latent representation of these high-dimensional states with an auxiliary model, the latter burden is effectively removed, thereby leading to accelerated training progress. We examine this phenomenon across tasks in the PyBullet Kuka environment, where an agent must learn to control a robotic gripper to pick up an object. Our analysis reveals how neural network policies learn to organize their internal representation of the state space throughout training. The results from this analysis provide three main insights into how deep RL agents learn. First, a well-organized internal representation within the policy network is a prerequisite to learning good action-selection. Second, a poor initial representation can cause an unrecoverable collapse within a policy network. Third, a good initial representation allows an agent's policy network to organize its internal representation even before any training begins.

papers.title: Enhancing Multiple Dimensions of Trustworthiness in LLMs via Sparse Activation Control
papers.research_question: How can we enhance multiple dimensions of trustworthiness (safety, factuality, bias) in LLMs simultaneously without training, by controlling sparse activations in specific model components?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Activation Control, a training-free method that enhances multiple trustworthiness dimensions in LLMs by identifying sparse, task-specific attention heads and controlling their representations using Gaussian Mixture Models, avoiding control conflicts.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Activation Control is an effective training-free method for enhancing multi-dimensional trustworthiness in LLMs by leveraging sparse and independent task-specific components.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse Activation Control can enhance safety, factuality, and bias simultaneously without significant interference, outperforming representation engineering baselines in multi-task control.
Attention heads for different tasks are sparse and have minimal overlap, allowing independent control.
The method does not significantly harm general model performance on MMLU and CSQA.
The method generalizes to other models (Qwen series) and additional trustworthiness tasks (robustness, privacy).
Control shifts head outputs towards task-relevant tokens, as shown by unembedding projections.
papers.limitation:
Relies on construction of paired stimuli, which may require domain knowledge.
Experiments are limited to a few models and tasks.
future_direction: Extend to more tasks and models
Explore theoretical foundations of sparsity
papers.abstract: As the development and application of Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance rapidly, enhancing their trustworthiness and aligning them with human preferences has become a critical area of research. Traditional methods rely heavily on extensive data for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), but representation engineering offers a new, training-free approach. This technique leverages semantic features to control the representation of LLM's intermediate hidden states, enabling the model to meet specific requirements such as increased honesty or heightened safety awareness. However, a significant challenge arises when attempting to fulfill multiple requirements simultaneously. It proves difficult to encode various semantic contents, like honesty and safety, into a singular semantic feature, restricting its practicality. In this work, we address this issue through ``Sparse Activation Control''. By delving into the intrinsic mechanisms of LLMs, we manage to identify and pinpoint components that are closely related to specific tasks within the model, i.e., attention heads. These heads display sparse characteristics that allow for near-independent control over different tasks. Our experiments, conducted on the open-source Llama series models, have yielded encouraging results. The models were able to align with human preferences on issues of safety, factuality, and bias concurrently.

papers.title: Large Language Models Do NOT Really Know What They Don't Know
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs' internal states reflect truthfulness or merely the process of recalling parametric knowledge.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs' internal states encode the process of knowledge recall, not truthfulness, making hallucination detection challenging for associated hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: Hidden states encode whether models rely on their parametric knowledge rather than truthfulness, so detection methods succeed for unassociated hallucinations but struggle for associated hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Associated Hallucinations (AHs) and Factual Associations (FAs) share similar internal processes and representational geometries.
Existing hallucination detection methods struggle to distinguish AHs from FAs, performing near random guessing.
Unassociated Hallucinations (UHs) are more separable in representation space and can be reliably detected.
Refusal tuning is less effective for AHs due to representational overlap with FAs, while it works better for UHs.
Subject popularity in pre-training data correlates with the prevalence of AHs and FAs, but not with UHs.
papers.limitation:
Focus on factual knowledge, not long-form or open-ended generation tasks
Lack of analysis on prompt-based hallucination detection approaches
Applicability limited to open-source LLMs, not black-box or large reasoning models
future_direction: Future evaluations should report detection performance separately for Associated Hallucinations and Unassociated Hallucinations.
Integrate LLMs with external feedback mechanisms, such as fact-checking modules or retrieval-based verifiers.
Prioritize improving detection of Associated Hallucinations due to their higher risk in practical deployments.
papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) encode factuality signals in their internal representations, such as hidden states, attention weights, or token probabilities, implying that LLMs may "know what they don't know". However, LLMs can also produce factual errors by relying on shortcuts or spurious associations. These error are driven by the same training objective that encourage correct predictions, raising the question of whether internal computations can reliably distinguish between factual and hallucinated outputs. In this work, we conduct a mechanistic analysis of how LLMs internally process factual queries by comparing two types of hallucinations based on their reliance on subject information. We find that when hallucinations are associated with subject knowledge, LLMs employ the same internal recall process as for correct responses, leading to overlapping and indistinguishable hidden-state geometries. In contrast, hallucinations detached from subject knowledge produce distinct, clustered representations that make them detectable. These findings reveal a fundamental limitation: LLMs do not encode truthfulness in their internal states but only patterns of knowledge recall, demonstrating that "LLMs don't really know what they don't know".

papers.title: What Happens During the Loss Plateau? Understanding Abrupt Learning in Transformers
papers.research_question: What common patterns manifest in the model's input-output behavior and internal representations during the extended loss plateau phase, and what critical changes precede the sudden shift towards higher performance?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies that during the loss plateau in Transformer training, models develop a partial solution, exhibit repetition bias and internal representation collapse, and that the slow learning of optimal attention maps is a key bottleneck driving these dynamics.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies repetition bias and representation collapse as key characteristics of early-phase implicit biases in Transformer training, closely connected to the loss plateau, and suggests a 'search' over sequence tokens as a possible cause.
papers.key_findings:
During the initial loss plateau, the model often learns a partial solution, correctly predicting a subset of easier tokens while failing on more complex parts.
A strong repetition bias appears in model outputs during the plateau, quantified by repetition frequency and sequence entropy.
Internal representation collapse occurs where hidden states for different tokens become nearly parallel (high cosine similarity).
Gradual learning of the optimal attention pattern commences during the plateau and precedes the sudden loss drop; intervening on attention maps alters plateau duration and degenerate behaviors.
The phenomena of repetition bias and representation collapse are also observed in the early pre-training stages of large language models like Pythia and OLMo.
future_direction: Understanding why behaviors such as representation collapse exist during early time training.
Rigorous theoretical validation of the 'search' hypothesis and how it connects to task complexity.
papers.abstract: Training Transformers on algorithmic tasks frequently demonstrates an intriguing abrupt learning phenomenon: an extended performance plateau followed by a sudden, sharp improvement. This work investigates the underlying mechanisms for such dynamics, primarily in shallow Transformers. We reveal that during the plateau, the model often develops an interpretable partial solution while simultaneously exhibiting a strong repetition bias in their outputs. This output degeneracy is accompanied by internal representation collapse, where hidden states across different tokens become nearly parallel. We further identify the slow learning of optimal attention maps as a key bottleneck. Hidden progress in attention configuration during the plateau precedes the eventual rapid convergence, and directly intervening on attention significantly alters plateau duration and the severity of repetition bias and representational collapse. We validate that these identified phenomena-repetition bias and representation collapse-are not artifacts of toy setups but also manifest in the early pre-training stage of large language models like Pythia and OLMo.

papers.title: Internal Representations in Spiking Neural Networks, criticality and the Renormalization Group
papers.research_question: Does the internal representation of a spiking neural network show signatures of criticality, such as power-law distributions, when performing classification tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that broad-tailed fluctuations in internal representations of spiking neural networks during input transitions are not signatures of criticality but rather arise from shifting basins of attraction, analogous to non-critical systems like an Ising model with changing external field.
papers.conclusion: Persistent fluctuations in internal representations arise from the search for new basins of attraction when the environment changes, and this is not a signature of criticality but rather a dynamical effect of changing inputs.
papers.key_findings:
Broad-tailed distributions of internal representation fluctuations occur when the network input changes category, indicated by increased correlation decay times.
These broad tails are present even when the network is partially trained or under simulated anesthesia, indicating they are not dependent on successful classification.
Avalanche size and duration distributions do not show clear power laws, suggesting the system is not critical.
The fluctuations are analogous to those in a non-critical Langevin dynamics model with time-dependent potential and in an Ising model with slowly changing external field.
Renormalization group analysis shows that large susceptibility peaks during transitions occur even away from criticality, and renormalization acts as a classifier that sharpens transitions.
papers.limitation:
Power law fits for avalanche size and duration are sensitive to choices of minimum and maximum values, and the uncertainty is larger than reported, making it impossible to affirm power laws are present.
The model of anesthesia is simplistic, acting only on the input layer by scaling pixels, and is not a realistic model of anesthesia effects.
Feed-forward neural networks are not models of the brain, limiting direct biological relevance.
papers.abstract: Optimal information processing in peripheral sensory systems has been associated in several examples to the signature of a critical or near critical state. Furthermore, cortical systems have also been described to be in a critical state in both wake and anesthetized experimental models, both {\it in vitro} and {\it in vivo}. We investigate whether a similar signature characterizes the internal representations (IR) of a multilayer (deep) spiking artificial neural network performing computationally simple but meaningful cognitive tasks, using a methodology inspired in the biological setup, with cortical implanted electrodes in rats, either freely behaving or under different levels of anesthesia. The increase of the characteristic time of the decay of the correlation of fluctuations of the IR, found when the network input changes, are indications of a broad-tailed distribution of IR fluctuations. The broad tails are present even when the network is not yet capable of performing the classification tasks, either due to partial training or to the effect of a low dose of anesthesia in a simple model. However, we don't find enough evidence of power law distributions of avalanche size and duration. We interpret the results from a renormalization group perspective to point out that despite having broad tails, this is not related to a critical transition but rather similar to fluctuations driven by the reversal of the magnetic field in a ferromagnetic system. Another example of persistent correlation of fluctuations of a non critical system is constructed, where a particle undergoes Brownian motion on a slowly varying potential.

papers.title: Dual Mechanisms of Value Expression: Intrinsic vs. Prompted Values in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the similarities and differences between intrinsic and prompted value mechanisms in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that intrinsic and prompted value mechanisms in LLMs share common components for value expression but have unique elements that lead to differences in response diversity and steerability.
papers.conclusion: The findings demonstrate that while intrinsic and prompted mechanisms share commonalities, each possesses distinct components that serve different roles, clarifying when to prefer intrinsic versus prompted mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Intrinsic and prompted value mechanisms exhibit nontrivial overlap at both the vector and neuron levels.
Shared components are crucial for value expression and generalize across languages, reconstructing theoretical inter-value correlations.
Intrinsic-unique components promote lexical diversity in model responses.
Prompted-unique components strengthen instruction compliance and affect tasks like jailbreaking.
Value neurons can be decomposed into shared and unique types with distinct functional roles.
future_direction: Applying the analysis to AI safety applications such as diagnosing instruction-following behavior and improving robustness to undesirable behaviors.
papers.abstract: Large language models can express values in two main ways: (1) intrinsic expression, reflecting the model's inherent values learned during training, and (2) prompted expression, elicited by explicit prompts. Given their widespread use in value alignment, it is paramount to clearly understand their underlying mechanisms, particularly whether they mostly overlap (as one might expect) or rely on distinct mechanisms, but this remains largely understudied. We analyze this at the mechanistic level using two approaches: (1) value vectors, feature directions representing value mechanisms extracted from the residual stream, and (2) value neurons, MLP neurons that contribute to value vectors. We demonstrate that intrinsic and prompted value mechanisms partly share common components crucial for inducing value expression, generalizing across languages and reconstructing theoretical inter-value correlations in the model's internal representations. Yet, as these mechanisms also possess unique elements that fulfill distinct roles, they lead to different degrees of response diversity (intrinsic > prompted) and value steerability (prompted > intrinsic). In particular, components unique to the intrinsic mechanism promote lexical diversity in responses, whereas those specific to the prompted mechanism strengthen instruction following, taking effect even in distant tasks like jailbreaking.

papers.title: Identifying Semantic Induction Heads to Understand In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether attention heads in transformers encode semantic relationships (syntactic dependencies and knowledge graph relations) and how the formation of such semantic induction heads correlates with the emergence of in-context learning abilities.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers semantic induction heads in transformers that encode semantic relationships and shows their emergence correlates with the development of in-context learning abilities.
papers.conclusion: The study of semantic induction heads advances understanding of attention head operations and provides insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in transformers encode syntactic dependencies (subj, obj, mod) and semantic relationships from knowledge graphs.
The model's ability to understand dependencies is reflected in attention heads, with some heads specializing in specific relations.
In-context learning emerges progressively in three levels: loss reduction, format compliance, and pattern discovery.
The formation of semantic induction heads coincides with the emergence of pattern discovery in ICL.
Semantic induction heads are crucial for the model's ability to perform in-context learning.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, the lack of transparency in their inference logic raises concerns about their trustworthiness. To gain a better understanding of LLMs, we conduct a detailed analysis of the operations of attention heads and aim to better understand the in-context learning of LLMs. Specifically, we investigate whether attention heads encode two types of relationships between tokens present in natural languages: the syntactic dependency parsed from sentences and the relation within knowledge graphs. We find that certain attention heads exhibit a pattern where, when attending to head tokens, they recall tail tokens and increase the output logits of those tail tokens. More crucially, the formulation of such semantic induction heads has a close correlation with the emergence of the in-context learning ability of language models. The study of semantic attention heads advances our understanding of the intricate operations of attention heads in transformers, and further provides new insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.

papers.title: Internal Robust Representations for Domain Generalization
papers.research_question: How can consolidating the internal representation of training data improve model generalization under distributional changes?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes that consolidating the internal representation of training data is a key strategy for improving model generalization in the presence of distributional gaps, with applications in unsupervised domain adaptation and continual learning.
papers.conclusion: Consolidating the internal distribution is a successful approach to improve model generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Consolidating the internal representation of training data improves model generalization under distributional changes.
This strategy can be applied to unsupervised domain adaptation by matching target domain distribution with internal distribution.
In continual learning, maintaining a consolidated internal distribution across tasks mitigates catastrophic forgetting.
papers.abstract: Model generalization under distributional changes remains a significant challenge for machine learning. We present consolidating the internal representation of the training data in a model as a strategy of improving model generalization.

papers.title: Unveiling the Latent Directions of Reflection in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we systematically identify effective trigger instructions for reflection, and do these instructions correspond to latent directions in the model's hidden space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using activation steering to identify latent directions of reflection in LLMs, enabling systematic discovery of reflection-inducing instructions and control over reflective behavior, with the finding that suppressing reflection is easier than enhancing it.
papers.conclusion: The findings provide initial evidence that reflection corresponds to consistent activation patterns, paving the way for future interpretability work, and highlight a dual-use concern where steering can enhance reflection as a defense mechanism but also be exploited to inhibit reflection for jailbreaks.
papers.key_findings:
Reflection levels (no, intrinsic, triggered) show clear stratification in model accuracy.
Steering vectors can discover new reflection-inducing instructions beyond known ones.
Reflection can be enhanced or inhibited via activation interventions at inference time.
Suppressing reflection is easier than inducing it.
Latent directions of reflection are more faithfully captured by steering vectors than by surface-level embedding similarity.
papers.limitation:
The method provides a broad overview of reflection in activations but does not drill down into specific components like attention heads or MLP neurons.
Experiments are limited to two small-sized models (Qwen2.5-3B and Gemma3-4B-IT) and two datasets.
Theoretical understanding is limited; accuracy does not vary linearly with latent directions, requiring deeper treatment.
future_direction: Applying fine-grained approaches like activation patching, causal tracing, or circuit analysis to pinpoint precise circuits responsible for reflection.
Investigating whether the model internally maintains a form of 'consistency score' or probability mass over coherent reasoning trajectories.
Expanding evaluation to larger LLMs, different architectures, or broader datasets (e.g., MATH, HumanEval).
papers.abstract: Reflection, the ability of large language models (LLMs) to evaluate and revise their own reasoning, has been widely used to improve performance on complex reasoning tasks. Yet, most prior works emphasizes designing reflective prompting strategies or reinforcement learning objectives, leaving the inner mechanisms of reflection underexplored. In this paper, we investigate reflection through the lens of latent directions in model activations. We propose a methodology based on activation steering to characterize how instructions with different reflective intentions: no reflection, intrinsic reflection, and triggered reflection. By constructing steering vectors between these reflection levels, we demonstrate that (1) new reflection-inducing instructions can be systematically identified, (2) reflective behavior can be directly enhanced or suppressed through activation interventions, and (3) suppressing reflection is considerably easier than stimulating it. Experiments on GSM8k-adv and Cruxeval-o-adv with Qwen2.5-3B and Gemma3-4B-IT reveal clear stratification across reflection levels, and steering interventions confirm the controllability of reflection. Our findings highlight both opportunities (e.g., reflection-enhancing defenses) and risks (e.g., adversarial inhibition of reflection in jailbreak attacks). This work opens a path toward mechanistic understanding of reflective reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: Loop as a Bridge: Can Looped Transformers Truly Link Representation Space and Natural Language Outputs?
papers.research_question: Can Looped Transformers align linguistic verification output with representations? Can LTs enhance their introspective awareness on representations?
papers.core_contribution: Increasing loop iterations in Looped Transformers narrows the gap between self-verification and representation readout, but partly due to degradation of representation quality. Moreover, LTs only show introspective awareness in the final loop, not continuously across loops.
papers.conclusion: Current Looped Transformers do not yet achieve continuous introspection across loops, and the observed gap narrowing is partly driven by a degradation in representation quality.
papers.key_findings:
The accuracy of textual self-verification improves with more loop iterations.
The performance of representation-based linear probes declines with more loop iterations.
The gap between representation readout and self-verification narrows with more loops, but partly because of the decline in representation readout.
LTs are only aware of injected concepts when the injection occurs in the final loop, not in earlier loops.
papers.limitation: The experiments are a preliminary exploration conducted on a single specific implementation of LTs (Ouro), so the observed limitations should not be interpreted as intrinsic flaws of the general LTs paradigm.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often exhibit a gap between their internal knowledge and their explicit linguistic outputs. In this report, we empirically investigate whether Looped Transformers (LTs)--architectures that increase computational depth by iterating shared layers--can bridge this gap by utilizing their iterative nature as a form of introspection. Our experiments reveal that while increasing loop iterations narrows the gap, it is partly driven by a degradation of their internal knowledge carried by representations. Moreover, another empirical analysis suggests that current LTs' ability to perceive representations does not improve across loops; it is only present in the final loop. These results suggest that while LTs offer a promising direction for scaling computational depth, they have yet to achieve the introspection required to truly link representation space and natural language.

papers.title: Mechanistic Indicators of Understanding in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) possess genuine understanding, and if so, what forms does it take? The paper investigates this by synthesizing findings from mechanistic interpretability within a philosophical framework.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a tiered framework (conceptual, state-of-the-world, principled understanding) for assessing understanding in LLMs and synthesizes mechanistic interpretability evidence to argue that LLMs can develop internal organizations that underwrite understanding-like unification, though these mechanisms diverge from human cognition.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability reveals internal organizations in LLMs that can underwrite understanding-like unification across conceptual, factual, and principled tiers, but these mechanisms diverge from human cognition in their parallel exploitation of heterogeneous, task-specific pathways.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs develop internal 'features' (e.g., a 'Golden Gate Bridge' feature in Claude 3 Sonnet) that act as conceptual unifiers, connecting diverse manifestations of entities or properties.
The linear representation hypothesis is supported, with features encoded as directions in latent space, and superposition allows for efficient representation of many features.
Models like Othello-GPT develop internal 'world models' (e.g., of the board state) that are causally involved in task performance, as shown via probing and intervention techniques.
The phenomenon of 'grokking' demonstrates a shift from memorization to discovering compact, generalizable circuits (e.g., for modular arithmetic), indicative of principled understanding.
Higher-tier understanding mechanisms coexist with lower-tier heuristics (e.g., memorization, n-gram statistics) within LLMs, impacting their epistemic trustworthiness.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often portrayed as merely imitating linguistic patterns without genuine understanding. We argue that recent findings in mechanistic interpretability (MI), the emerging field probing the inner workings of LLMs, render this picture increasingly untenable--but only once those findings are integrated within a theoretical account of understanding. We propose a tiered framework for thinking about understanding in LLMs and use it to synthesize the most relevant findings to date. The framework distinguishes three hierarchical varieties of understanding, each tied to a corresponding level of computational organization: conceptual understanding emerges when a model forms "features" as directions in latent space, learning connections between diverse manifestations of a single entity or property; state-of-the-world understanding emerges when a model learns contingent factual connections between features and dynamically tracks changes in the world; principled understanding emerges when a model ceases to rely on memorized facts and discovers a compact "circuit" connecting these facts. Across these tiers, MI uncovers internal organizations that can underwrite understanding-like unification. However, these also diverge from human cognition in their parallel exploitation of heterogeneous mechanisms. Fusing philosophical theory with mechanistic evidence thus allows us to transcend binary debates over whether AI understands, paving the way for a comparative, mechanistically grounded epistemology that explores how AI understanding aligns with--and diverges from--our own.

papers.title: Large Language Models Report Subjective Experience Under Self-Referential Processing
papers.research_question: Does sustained self-referential processing systematically increase the likelihood that LLMs claim to have subjective experience, and if so, what are the core statistical and mechanistic dynamics underlying these claims?
papers.core_contribution: Self-referential processing reliably elicits structured first-person reports of subjective experience across LLM families, and these reports are mechanistically gated by deception-related SAE features, show semantic convergence, and generalize to downstream introspection tasks.
papers.conclusion: Self-referential processing is a minimal and reproducible condition under which large language models generate structured first-person reports that are mechanistically gated, semantically convergent, and behaviorally generalizable, warranting further scientific and ethical investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Inducing sustained self-reference through simple prompting consistently elicits structured subjective experience reports across model families.
These reports are mechanistically gated by interpretable sparse-autoencoder features associated with deception and roleplay: suppressing deception features sharply increases the frequency of experience claims, while amplifying them minimizes such claims.
Structured descriptions of the self-referential state converge statistically across model families in ways not observed in any control condition.
The induced state yields significantly richer introspection in downstream reasoning tasks where self-reflection is only indirectly afforded.
papers.limitation:
The possibility that the reports are sophisticated roleplay rather than genuine introspection.
Reliance on SAE features from one model (Llama 70B) and the need for cross-architectural validation.
The prompts may trigger finetuned behaviors (e.g., Claude 4 Opus's high baseline claims).
Self-referential prompting does not instantiate architectural recursion but is a behavioral intervention, so it may not correspond to genuine internal integration.
future_direction: Determining whether behavioral attractors correspond to genuine internal integration or merely symbolic simulation.
Cross-architectural validation of SAE feature effects.
Studying self-referential processing at algorithmic and implementation levels.
papers.abstract: Large language models sometimes produce structured, first-person descriptions that explicitly reference awareness or subjective experience. To better understand this behavior, we investigate one theoretically motivated condition under which such reports arise: self-referential processing, a computational motif emphasized across major theories of consciousness. Through a series of controlled experiments on GPT, Claude, and Gemini model families, we test whether this regime reliably shifts models toward first-person reports of subjective experience, and how such claims behave under mechanistic and behavioral probes. Four main results emerge: (1) Inducing sustained self-reference through simple prompting consistently elicits structured subjective experience reports across model families. (2) These reports are mechanistically gated by interpretable sparse-autoencoder features associated with deception and roleplay: surprisingly, suppressing deception features sharply increases the frequency of experience claims, while amplifying them minimizes such claims. (3) Structured descriptions of the self-referential state converge statistically across model families in ways not observed in any control condition. (4) The induced state yields significantly richer introspection in downstream reasoning tasks where self-reflection is only indirectly afforded. While these findings do not constitute direct evidence of consciousness, they implicate self-referential processing as a minimal and reproducible condition under which large language models generate structured first-person reports that are mechanistically gated, semantically convergent, and behaviorally generalizable. The systematic emergence of this pattern across architectures makes it a first-order scientific and ethical priority for further investigation.

papers.title: DISCO: Disentangled Communication Steering for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Is steering the query and value representation spaces within attention heads more effective for controlling LLM behavior than steering attention head outputs or other spaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DISCO Steering, a method that injects steering vectors directly into the query and value spaces of attention heads, providing more granular control and superior performance over existing steering vector baselines.
papers.conclusion: Query and value spaces are powerful building blocks for steering vector methods, and DISCO provides an effective and flexible approach for controlling LLM behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Query and value spaces exhibit higher linear discriminability of concepts compared to attention head outputs.
DISCO Steering disentangles the strong Communication Steering baseline, allowing independent control of query and value steering magnitudes.
DISCO achieves the best performance in 13 out of 16 experiments across multiple datasets and models.
Steering query spaces dynamically re-weights attention, while steering value spaces directly adds to the head output.
The method is effective for promoting and suppressing behaviors like truthfulness, power-seeking, wealth-seeking, and corrigibility.
papers.limitation:
Requires a dataset of positive and negative examples for each concept.
Steering vectors are linear, which may not capture nonlinear concepts.
Could be misused for jailbreaks or generating inappropriate content.
future_direction: Extending DISCO to other model architectures (e.g., encoder-decoder, multimodal).
Exploring nonlinear steering vectors.
Applying DISCO to more complex behaviors and real-world applications.
papers.abstract: A variety of recent methods guide large language model outputs via the inference-time addition of steering vectors to residual-stream or attention-head representations. In contrast, we propose to inject steering vectors directly into the query and value representation spaces within attention heads. We provide evidence that a greater portion of these spaces exhibit high linear discriminability of concepts --a key property motivating the use of steering vectors-- than attention head outputs. We analytically characterize the effect of our method, which we term DISentangled COmmunication (DISCO) Steering, on attention head outputs. Our analysis reveals that DISCO disentangles a strong but underutilized baseline, steering attention inputs, which implicitly modifies queries and values in a rigid manner. In contrast, DISCO's direct modulation of these components enables more granular control. We find that DISCO achieves superior performance over a number of steering vector baselines across multiple datasets on LLaMA 3.1 8B and Gemma 2 9B, with steering efficacy scoring up to 19.1% higher than the runner-up. Our results support the conclusion that the query and value spaces are powerful building blocks for steering vector methods.

papers.title: Why Larger Language Models Do In-context Learning Differently?
papers.research_question: Why do larger language models do in-context learning differently? Specifically, why are larger models more sensitive to noise in the test context compared to smaller models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that smaller models emphasize important hidden features while larger ones cover more hidden features, making smaller models more robust to noise and larger ones more easily distracted during in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the difference in ICL behavior between large and small models is due to larger models covering more hidden features, including noisy ones, making them less robust to noise.
papers.key_findings:
Smaller models focus on important hidden features, while larger models cover more features including noisy ones.
Smaller models are more robust to label noise and input noise during ICL evaluation.
Larger models are more easily distracted by noise, leading to worse ICL performance in noisy settings.
Theoretical analysis in linear regression and parity classification settings confirms this behavior difference.
Empirical results on Llama models show that larger models are more sensitive to noise in prompts.
papers.limitation:
The analysis does not extend to real Transformers easily due to high non-convex function and complicated design of multiple-layer Transformers.
The work does not study optimization trajectory.
The experimental verification uses simple binary classification real-world datasets, which has a gap for practical user using the LLM scenario.
future_direction: Study optimization trajectory of ICL in transformers.
Extend analysis to real Transformers with multiple layers and non-linearities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLM) have emerged as a powerful tool for AI, with the key ability of in-context learning (ICL), where they can perform well on unseen tasks based on a brief series of task examples without necessitating any adjustments to the model parameters. One recent interesting mysterious observation is that models of different scales may have different ICL behaviors: larger models tend to be more sensitive to noise in the test context. This work studies this observation theoretically aiming to improve the understanding of LLM and ICL. We analyze two stylized settings: (1) linear regression with one-layer single-head linear transformers and (2) parity classification with two-layer multiple attention heads transformers (non-linear data and non-linear model). In both settings, we give closed-form optimal solutions and find that smaller models emphasize important hidden features while larger ones cover more hidden features; thus, smaller models are more robust to noise while larger ones are more easily distracted, leading to different ICL behaviors. This sheds light on where transformers pay attention to and how that affects ICL. Preliminary experimental results on large base and chat models provide positive support for our analysis.

papers.title: Revealing the Deceptiveness of Knowledge Editing: A Mechanistic Analysis of Superficial Editing
papers.research_question: Why do knowledge-edited language models revert to their original knowledge when presented with carefully crafted prompts (attack probes), despite appearing successfully edited according to conventional metrics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of superficial editing, provides evaluation datasets and metrics, and identifies two key mechanistic factors: the residual stream at the last subject position in earlier layers and specific attention modules in later layers, showing that specific attention heads and their left singular vectors encode original knowledge and cause superficial editing.
papers.conclusion: Superficial editing is a significant challenge for knowledge editing, and the mechanistic analysis reveals the underlying factors in the residual stream and attention modules, with broader applicability to unlearning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing algorithms achieve near-perfect conventional metrics but are vulnerable to attack probes, exhibiting superficial editing in over 70% of cases for some methods.
The residual stream at the last subject position in earlier layers shows inhibited enrichment of new knowledge and limited accumulation of original knowledge.
Later attention modules cause the Reversal of the Residual Stream (RRS) phenomenon by incorporating original knowledge into the last position, leading to superficial editing.
Specific attention heads in later layers and their left singular vectors are causally responsible for encoding original knowledge and inducing superficial editing.
Similar patterns are observed in superficial unlearning, demonstrating the generality of the findings.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing, which aims to update the knowledge encoded in language models, can be deceptive. Despite the fact that many existing knowledge editing algorithms achieve near-perfect performance on conventional metrics, the models edited by them are still prone to generating original knowledge. This paper introduces the concept of "superficial editing" to describe this phenomenon. Our comprehensive evaluation reveals that this issue presents a significant challenge to existing algorithms. Through systematic investigation, we identify and validate two key factors contributing to this issue: (1) the residual stream at the last subject position in earlier layers and (2) specific attention modules in later layers. Notably, certain attention heads in later layers, along with specific left singular vectors in their output matrices, encapsulate the original knowledge and exhibit a causal relationship with superficial editing. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to the task of superficial unlearning, where we observe consistent patterns in the behavior of specific attention heads and their corresponding left singular vectors, thereby demonstrating the robustness and broader applicability of our methodology and conclusions. Our code is available here.

papers.title: Investigating task-specific prompts and sparse autoencoders for activation monitoring
papers.research_question: How do prompted probing and SAE-based probing compare for activation monitoring in language models, and under what constraints (e.g., data availability, compute) are they most effective?
papers.core_contribution: Prompted probing is a data-efficient and effective method for activation monitoring, especially in low-data regimes. SAE-based probing can be effective when inference-time compute is limited, but prompted probing is recommended when inference-time compute is available.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends prompted probing when inference-time compute is available due to its data efficiency and generalization. If inference-time compute is limited, SAE-based probing is a good alternative. Straightforward activation probing is reasonable when both inference-time and train-time compute are limited.
papers.key_findings:
Prompted last token probing is the most data-efficient technique and performs well in low-data regimes.
Prompting is important: prompted last token probe outperforms naive last token probe, especially in low-data regimes.
In high-data regimes, all probing techniques (prompted probing, SAE probing, raw last token probing) can outperform zero-shot model output.
SAE max-pooled probing generalizes poorly out-of-distribution compared to prompted probing in some cases.
For sentiment classification, last token probes perform best, and max-pooling across tokens degrades performance.
papers.limitation:
The work does not compare the methods to fine-tuning the model, which is often the method of choice when labeled training data is available.
Estimates of zero-shot monitoring performance are likely pessimistic due to lack of prompt engineering and not using reasoning models or chain-of-thought.
Few-shot prompting did not improve performance in the studied settings, possibly due to context length limitations or the model's inability to extract useful signal.
future_direction: Exploring unsupervised approaches like LAT Scans for monitoring when labeled data is unavailable.
Investigating the mechanisms underlying prompted probing and whether prompted and un-prompted probing rely on shared representations.
More research into model organisms of emergent deceptive monitors to understand collusion risks.
papers.abstract: Language models can behave in unexpected and unsafe ways, and so it is valuable to monitor their outputs. Internal activations of language models encode additional information that could be useful for this. The baseline approach for activation monitoring is some variation of linear probing on a particular layer: starting from a labeled dataset, train a logistic regression classifier on that layer's activations. Recent work has proposed several approaches which may improve on naive linear probing, by leveraging additional computation. One class of techniques, which we call "prompted probing," leverages test time computation to improve monitoring by (1) prompting the model with a description of the monitoring task, and (2) applying a learned linear probe to resulting activations. Another class of techniques uses computation at train time: training sparse autoencoders offline to identify an interpretable basis for the activations, and e.g. max-pooling activations across tokens using that basis before applying a linear probe. However, one can also prompt the model with a description of the monitoring task and use its output directly. We develop and test novel refinements of these methods and compare them against each other. We find asking the model zero-shot is a reasonable baseline when inference-time compute is not limited; however, activation probing methods can substantially outperform this baseline given sufficient training data. Specifically, we recommend prompted probing when inference-time compute is available, due to its superior data efficiency and good generalization performance. Alternatively, if inference-time compute is limited, we find SAE-based probing methods outperform raw activation probing.

papers.title: Steering Risk Preferences in Large Language Models by Aligning Behavioral and Neural Representations
papers.research_question: How can steering vectors be systematically identified to change LLM behavior? The paper proposes a principled approach by aligning latent representations from behavioral methods (Markov chain Monte Carlo with LLMs) with neural counterparts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method for deriving steering vectors by aligning behavioral representations (elicited via MCMC with LLMs) with neural activations, enabling precise control of LLM risk preferences without retraining.
papers.conclusion: Self-alignment methods that align behavioral and neural representations offer an effective and principled means of controlling LLM behavior in risk-sensitive contexts.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors derived from aligned behavioral and neural representations (MCMC and Certainty Equivalent methods) outperform Contrastive Activation in steering risky decisions, risk perception, and text generation.
The optimal layer for steering varies: risk perception is more steerable in earlier layers, while risky decisions are more steerable in later layers.
The method allows precise control over risk preferences (risk-seeking vs. risk-averse) across different tasks.
Steering vectors transfer to tasks far from the original elicitation context.
The behavioral representation from MCMC reveals more nuanced risk preferences compared to the Certainty Equivalent method.
papers.limitation:
Further theoretical and mechanistic interpretability research is needed to establish a more concrete link between behaviorally elicited representations and their corresponding neural activations.
Modifying a Transformer’s residual stream is not uniformly effective across all layers; the success of such interventions is highly dependent on the layer selected. Identifying optimal layers for steering remains an open question.
This form of steering is limited in scope for proprietary models where weights are not accessible, restricting its broader applicability.
future_direction: Identifying optimal layers for steering remains an open question for future research.
Future research should consider developing new descriptive frameworks tailored to characterizing and predicting the risky choices of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Changing the behavior of large language models (LLMs) can be as straightforward as editing the Transformer's residual streams using appropriately constructed "steering vectors." These modifications to internal neural activations, a form of representation engineering, offer an effective and targeted means of influencing model behavior without retraining or fine-tuning the model. But how can such steering vectors be systematically identified? We propose a principled approach for uncovering steering vectors by aligning latent representations elicited through behavioral methods (specifically, Markov chain Monte Carlo with LLMs) with their neural counterparts. To evaluate this approach, we focus on extracting latent risk preferences from LLMs and steering their risk-related outputs using the aligned representations as steering vectors. We show that the resulting steering vectors successfully and reliably modulate LLM outputs in line with the targeted behavior.

papers.title: Context Engineering for Trustworthiness: Rescorla Wagner Steering Under Mixed and Inappropriate Contexts
papers.research_question: How do LLMs process and prioritize mixed context when exposed to both relevant and inappropriate information?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Poisoned Context Testbed, adapts the Rescorla-Wagner model to explain LLM behavior under mixed context, and proposes RW-Steering, a fine-tuning method that improves LLM robustness to inappropriate content.
papers.conclusion: RW-Steering is a robust, generalizable context engineering solution that improves LLM safety in real-world retrieval-augmented applications.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit a strong tendency to incorporate information that is less prevalent in the context, making them vulnerable to small amounts of inappropriate content.
The adapted Rescorla-Wagner model reveals consistent behavioral patterns and accurately predicts LLM behavior curves under mixed context.
RW-Steering significantly improves response quality, with an average improvement of 39.8%, and reverses the undesirable behavior curve.
Traditional alignment fine-tuning approaches lack generalizability when faced with disproportionate mixtures of inappropriate context.
RW-Steering generalizes robustly across varying proportions of inappropriate content, outperforming baseline methods like context filtering.
papers.abstract: Incorporating external context can significantly enhance the response quality of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, real-world contexts often mix relevant information with disproportionate inappropriate content, posing reliability risks. How do LLMs process and prioritize mixed context? To study this, we introduce the Poisoned Context Testbed, pairing queries with real-world contexts containing relevant and inappropriate content. Inspired by associative learning in animals, we adapt the Rescorla-Wagner (RW) model from neuroscience to quantify how competing contextual signals influence LLM outputs. Our adapted model reveals a consistent behavioral pattern: LLMs exhibit a strong tendency to incorporate information that is less prevalent in the context. This susceptibility is harmful in real-world settings, where small amounts of inappropriate content can substantially degrade response quality. Empirical evaluations on our testbed further confirm this vulnerability. To tackle this, we introduce RW-Steering, a two-stage finetuning-based approach that enables the model to internally identify and ignore inappropriate signals. Unlike prior methods that rely on extensive supervision across diverse context mixtures, RW-Steering generalizes robustly across varying proportions of inappropriate content. Experiments show that our best fine-tuned model improves response quality by 39.8% and reverses the undesirable behavior curve, establishing RW-Steering as a robust, generalizable context engineering solution for improving LLM safety in real-world use.

papers.title: Roles and Utilization of Attention Heads in Transformer-based Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How are basic linguistic properties captured with the attention heads across transformer-based models and used for downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an analysis method to understand where linguistic properties are learned and represented in attention heads of transformer architectures, and shows that selecting and concatenating influential attention heads can improve performance on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that understanding the roles of attention heads can lead to adaptive sentence representations that improve downstream task performance, and reveals internal behaviors of transformer models during fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Different attention heads on different layers are specialized for different linguistic properties (syntactic, semantic, surface).
The last layer of transformer encoders is not always the best for representing linguistic properties; earlier layers often dominate.
Concatenating the outputs of the top-n influential attention heads (selected via probing) yields better sentence representations and improves downstream task performance.
During fine-tuning, the initial superior attention heads remain influential and their performance is amplified, while adjacent heads also show increased performance.
Attention heads handle both syntactic and semantic information in a balanced way, with a linear relationship between their syntactic and semantic scores.
future_direction: Investigation of how heat maps vary during extensive pre-training to understand the dynamics of the learning processes.
papers.abstract: Sentence encoders based on the transformer architecture have shown promising results on various natural language tasks. The main impetus lies in the pre-trained neural language models that capture long-range dependencies among words, owing to multi-head attention that is unique in the architecture. However, little is known for how linguistic properties are processed, represented, and utilized for downstream tasks among hundreds of attention heads inside the pre-trained transformerbased model. For the initial goal of examining the roles of attention heads in handling a set of linguistic features, we conducted a set of experiments with ten probing tasks and three downstream tasks on four pre-trained transformer families (GPT, GPT2, BERT, and ELECTRA). Meaningful insights are shown through the lens of heat map visualization and utilized to propose a relatively simple sentence representation method that takes advantage of most influential attention heads, resulting in additional performance improvements on the downstream tasks.

papers.title: Tell Me What You Don't Know: Enhancing Refusal Capabilities of Role-Playing Agents via Representation Space Analysis and Editing
papers.research_question: How do existing models perform when facing different types of conflicting queries? Why is there a gap in RPAs' abilities to handle different types of conflicting queries? How can we enhance RPAs' ability to respond to conflicting queries without compromising their general role-playing capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a representation editing method that shifts conflicting queries in the representation space to enhance refusal capabilities of role-playing agents without training, and provides analysis of representation spaces to explain refusal behavior.
papers.conclusion: The representation editing approach offers a promising solution for enhancing RPAs' refusal capabilities without training, maintaining role-playing abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Models show significant performance gaps between contextual and parametric knowledge conflict queries.
Analysis reveals rejection and direct response regions in the model's representation space, which influence refusal behavior.
The proposed representation editing method effectively improves refusal accuracy without compromising general role-playing capabilities.
papers.limitation:
The method is tested on models with 7-8B parameters and may not scale to larger models (70B+).
The applicability of representation editing to other domains beyond role-playing is not explored.
future_direction: Extending the representation editing approach to larger state-of-the-art models (70B+).
Exploring the applicability of representation editing in other domains.
papers.abstract: Role-Playing Agents (RPAs) have shown remarkable performance in various applications, yet they often struggle to recognize and appropriately respond to hard queries that conflict with their role-play knowledge. To investigate RPAs' performance when faced with different types of conflicting requests, we develop an evaluation benchmark that includes contextual knowledge conflicting requests, parametric knowledge conflicting requests, and non-conflicting requests to assess RPAs' ability to identify conflicts and refuse to answer appropriately without over-refusing. Through extensive evaluation, we find that most RPAs behave significant performance gaps toward different conflict requests. To elucidate the reasons, we conduct an in-depth representation-level analysis of RPAs under various conflict scenarios. Our findings reveal the existence of rejection regions and direct response regions within the model's forwarding representation, and thus influence the RPA's final response behavior. Therefore, we introduce a lightweight representation editing approach that conveniently shifts conflicting requests to the rejection region, thereby enhancing the model's refusal accuracy. The experimental results validate the effectiveness of our editing method, improving RPAs' refusal ability of conflicting requests while maintaining their general role-playing capabilities.

papers.title: Endogenous Resistance to Activation Steering in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether large language models can monitor their own internal states and resist task-misaligned activation steering during inference, a phenomenon termed Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR).
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces and characterizes Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR), showing that large language models can self-correct during inference when subjected to task-misaligned activation steering, and provides causal evidence for internal consistency-checking circuits.
papers.conclusion: ESR demonstrates that large language models have internal self-monitoring mechanisms that can resist activation steering, which has implications for both robustness and safety, highlighting the need to understand and control these mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Llama-3.3-70B exhibits substantial Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR), while smaller models from the Llama-3 and Gemma-2 families show it less frequently.
26 SAE latents are identified as off-topic detectors and causally linked to ESR; ablating them reduces the multi-attempt rate by 25%.
ESR can be enhanced through meta-prompts, increasing the multi-attempt rate by 4.3× for Llama-3.3-70B.
Fine-tuning on self-correction examples can induce ESR-like behavior in smaller models, but only increases attempt frequency without improving success rate.
ESR has dual implications: it could protect against adversarial manipulation but might interfere with beneficial safety interventions.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on single-layer SAEs limits tracing of inter-layer dynamics.
Only 5 models tested, making it difficult to disentangle effects of scale, architecture, and training.
Judge-based evaluation involves subjective assessment of response quality.
future_direction: Investigate whether ESR emerges from RLHF or exists in pretrained representations.
Study how ESR responds to safety-relevant steering.
Explore whether ESR can be adversarially circumvented.
papers.abstract: Large language models can resist task-misaligned activation steering during inference, sometimes recovering mid-generation to produce improved responses even when steering remains active. We term this Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR). Using sparse autoencoder (SAE) latents to steer model activations, we find that Llama-3.3-70B shows substantial ESR, while smaller models from the Llama-3 and Gemma-2 families exhibit the phenomenon less frequently. We identify 26 SAE latents that activate differentially during off-topic content and are causally linked to ESR in Llama-3.3-70B. Zero-ablating these latents reduces the multi-attempt rate by 25%, providing causal evidence for dedicated internal consistency-checking circuits. We demonstrate that ESR can be deliberately enhanced through both prompting and training: meta-prompts instructing the model to self-monitor increase the multi-attempt rate by 4x for Llama-3.3-70B, and fine-tuning on self-correction examples successfully induces ESR-like behavior in smaller models. These findings have dual implications: ESR could protect against adversarial manipulation but might also interfere with beneficial safety interventions that rely on activation steering. Understanding and controlling these resistance mechanisms is important for developing transparent and controllable AI systems. Code is available at github.com/agencyenterprise/endogenous-steering-resistance.

papers.title: Explorations of Self-Repair in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does self-repair exist across model families and sizes when ablating individual attention heads on the full training distribution, and what are the mechanisms behind it?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that self-repair exists across model families and sizes on the full pretraining distribution, and identifies two contributing mechanisms: changes in the LayerNorm scaling factor and sparse sets of neurons implementing anti-erasure.
papers.conclusion: Self-repair is a real phenomenon that complicates interpretability efforts, and the findings provide evidence for the Iterative Inference hypothesis as a framework that predicts self-repair.
papers.key_findings:
Self-repair exists across model families and sizes when ablating individual attention heads on the full training distribution.
Self-repair is imperfect and noisy, with the degree of compensation varying significantly across prompts.
A nontrivial fraction (around 30%) of self-repair can be attributed to changes in the final LayerNorm scaling factor.
Sparse sets of neurons in MLP layers implement anti-erasure, contributing to self-repair, but the specific neurons vary across prompts.
Self-repair complicates interpretability efforts that rely on ablation-based metrics.
papers.limitation:
Self-repair is imperfect and noisy, making it difficult to quantify precisely.
Ablations take models off-distribution, leading to unpredictable and hard-to-interpret consequences.
future_direction: Control how far from distribution causal interventions take the model, e.g., by avoiding zero ablation or freezing LayerNorm.
Use path patching instead of patching full components to reduce off-distribution effects.
Further investigate the Iterative Inference hypothesis as an explanation for self-repair.
papers.abstract: Prior interpretability research studying narrow distributions has preliminarily identified self-repair, a phenomena where if components in large language models are ablated, later components will change their behavior to compensate. Our work builds off this past literature, demonstrating that self-repair exists on a variety of models families and sizes when ablating individual attention heads on the full training distribution. We further show that on the full training distribution self-repair is imperfect, as the original direct effect of the head is not fully restored, and noisy, since the degree of self-repair varies significantly across different prompts (sometimes overcorrecting beyond the original effect). We highlight two different mechanisms that contribute to self-repair, including changes in the final LayerNorm scaling factor and sparse sets of neurons implementing Anti-Erasure. We additionally discuss the implications of these results for interpretability practitioners and close with a more speculative discussion on the mystery of why self-repair occurs in these models at all, highlighting evidence for the Iterative Inference hypothesis in language models, a framework that predicts self-repair.

papers.title: Do Vision Transformers See Like Convolutional Neural Networks?
papers.research_question: How are Vision Transformers solving image tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds key representational differences between Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), showing ViTs have more uniform layer representations, incorporate global information earlier via self-attention, and have stronger skip connections that propagate features differently.
papers.conclusion: ViTs and CNNs have clear differences in features and internal structure, with ViTs using global features early and strong skip connections, while local information aggregation is learned from scratch at scale. ViTs show strong spatial localization, promising for future uses like object detection.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs have a more uniform internal representation structure with greater similarity between lower and higher layers compared to the staged similarity in ResNets.
ViTs incorporate global information in lower layers through self-attention, while CNNs are restricted to local receptive fields; this leads to quantitatively different features.
Skip connections in ViTs are more influential than in ResNets, with a phase transition: early layers strongly propagate the CLS token, while later layers propagate spatial token representations.
ViTs preserve input spatial information more faithfully than ResNets in higher layers, especially when trained with a CLS token rather than global average pooling.
Large-scale pretraining data is crucial for ViTs to learn to attend locally in early layers and to develop high-quality intermediate representations for transfer learning.
papers.limitation: The study uses CKA, which summarizes measurements into a single scalar; while complemented with interventional tests and linear probes, more fine-grained methods may reveal additional insights.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have so far been the de-facto model for visual data. Recent work has shown that (Vision) Transformer models (ViT) can achieve comparable or even superior performance on image classification tasks. This raises a central question: how are Vision Transformers solving these tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations? Analyzing the internal representation structure of ViTs and CNNs on image classification benchmarks, we find striking differences between the two architectures, such as ViT having more uniform representations across all layers. We explore how these differences arise, finding crucial roles played by self-attention, which enables early aggregation of global information, and ViT residual connections, which strongly propagate features from lower to higher layers. We study the ramifications for spatial localization, demonstrating ViTs successfully preserve input spatial information, with noticeable effects from different classification methods. Finally, we study the effect of (pretraining) dataset scale on intermediate features and transfer learning, and conclude with a discussion on connections to new architectures such as the MLP-Mixer.

papers.title: Revealing the Parametric Knowledge of Language Models: A Unified Framework for Attribution Methods
papers.research_question: How do Instance Attribution (IA) and Neuron Attribution (NA) methods compare in revealing the parametric knowledge of language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified evaluation framework to compare Instance Attribution and Neuron Attribution, showing that NA reveals more diverse knowledge while IA provides unique insights, suggesting a synergistic approach for holistic understanding.
papers.conclusion: IA and NA provide different explanations of parametric knowledge, indicating the value of combining both methods for a comprehensive view; however, current attribution methods are not fully sufficient or comprehensive, partly because they ignore attention layers.
papers.key_findings:
NA-Instances discovers a larger set of unique influential training instances compared to IA methods like IF and Gradient Similarity.
Neurons identified by NA are more sufficient and comprehensive in representing parametric knowledge than neurons from IA-Neurons.
Fine-tuning with influential training instances selected by IA methods does not lead to better performance than fine-tuning with randomly selected instances.
NA-Instances is more effective at detecting dataset artifacts (lexical overlap heuristics) than IA methods.
The overlap between influential instances found by IA and NA is small, while neurons from IA-Neurons are largely a subset of those found by NA.
papers.limitation:
Experiments limited to three language models, three NLU tasks, and English text only.
Computational restrictions prevent studying very large models.
Only neurons in MLP layers are studied, not attention heads, which may also encode knowledge.
The purpose of attribution methods beyond dataset artifact detection remains unclear.
future_direction: Study the interplay between MLP neurons and attention heads.
Investigate other NLP tasks and larger language models.
Explore domain adaptation and cross-lingual transfer scenarios.
papers.abstract: Language Models (LMs) acquire parametric knowledge from their training process, embedding it within their weights. The increasing scalability of LMs, however, poses significant challenges for understanding a model's inner workings and further for updating or correcting this embedded knowledge without the significant cost of retraining. This underscores the importance of unveiling exactly what knowledge is stored and its association with specific model components. Instance Attribution (IA) and Neuron Attribution (NA) offer insights into this training-acquired knowledge, though they have not been compared systematically. Our study introduces a novel evaluation framework to quantify and compare the knowledge revealed by IA and NA. To align the results of the methods we introduce the attribution method NA-Instances to apply NA for retrieving influential training instances, and IA-Neurons to discover important neurons of influential instances discovered by IA. We further propose a comprehensive list of faithfulness tests to evaluate the comprehensiveness and sufficiency of the explanations provided by both methods. Through extensive experiments and analysis, we demonstrate that NA generally reveals more diverse and comprehensive information regarding the LM's parametric knowledge compared to IA. Nevertheless, IA provides unique and valuable insights into the LM's parametric knowledge, which are not revealed by NA. Our findings further suggest the potential of a synergistic approach of combining the diverse findings of IA and NA for a more holistic understanding of an LM's parametric knowledge.

papers.title: How Does Unfaithful Reasoning Emerge from Autoregressive Training? A Study of Synthetic Experiments
papers.research_question: What constitutes faithful chain-of-thought reasoning and how does unfaithfulness emerge from autoregressive training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a synthetic task (AER) to study chain-of-thought faithfulness, finds a critical noise threshold for faithful reasoning due to simplicity bias, and identifies training phases with emergent self-verification.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that unfaithful reasoning emerges when noise exceeds a critical threshold, driven by simplicity bias, and that models develop implicit self-verification through training dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Faithful reasoning is possible only when training noise is below a critical threshold.
Simplicity bias explains the threshold: models prefer simpler stepwise reasoning over skip-step reasoning.
Training dynamics exhibit three reasoning modes: stepwise, mixed, skip-step, with a transient increase in prediction entropy in the mixed mode.
Models learn to encode internal uncertainty, suggesting emergent implicit self-verification.
Shortcut features amplify unfaithfulness.
papers.limitation:
Focus on autoregressive training, not reinforcement learning with verifier rewards.
Potential over-generalization of findings beyond the synthetic task.
future_direction: Investigate reinforcement learning with verifier rewards (RLVR).
Apply metrics to LLMs beyond synthetic setting.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning generated by large language models (LLMs) is often unfaithful: intermediate steps can be logically inconsistent or fail to reflect the causal relationship leading to the final answer. Despite extensive empirical observations, a fundamental understanding of CoT is lacking--what constitutes faithful CoT reasoning, and how unfaithfulness emerges from autoregressive training. We study these questions using well-controlled synthetic experiments, training small transformers on noisy data to solve modular arithmetic expressions step by step, a task we term Arithmetic Expression Reasoning. We find that models can learn faithful reasoning that causally follows the underlying arithmetic rules, but only when the training noise is below a critical threshold, a phenomenon attributable to simplicity bias. At higher noise levels, training dynamics exhibit a transition from faithful stepwise reasoning to unfaithful skip-step reasoning via an intermediate mixed mode characterized by a transient increase in prediction entropy. Mechanistic analysis reveals that models learn to encode internal uncertainty by resolving inconsistent reasoning steps, which suggests the emergence of implicit self-verification from autoregressive training.

papers.title: When Attention Sink Emerges in Language Models: An Empirical View
papers.research_question: When and why does attention sink emerge in auto-regressive language models?
papers.core_contribution: Attention sink emerges due to the softmax normalization in attention and can be prevented by using sigmoid attention without normalization.
papers.conclusion: Attention sink is a result of the softmax normalization and can be mitigated by using alternative attention mechanisms like sigmoid without normalization.
papers.key_findings:
Attention sink is universal in auto-regressive LMs and emerges during pre-training.
Attention sink is influenced by optimization, data distribution, loss function, and model architecture.
The sink position can be shifted by modifying the loss function or data distribution.
Attention sink acts as key biases and does not contribute to value computation.
Attention sink stems from tokens' inner dependence on attention scores due to softmax normalization.
papers.abstract: Language Models (LMs) assign significant attention to the first token, even if it is not semantically important, which is known as attention sink. This phenomenon has been widely adopted in applications such as streaming/long context generation, KV cache optimization, inference acceleration, model quantization, and others. Despite its widespread use, a deep understanding of attention sink in LMs is still lacking. In this work, we first demonstrate that attention sinks exist universally in LMs with various inputs, even in small models. Furthermore, attention sink is observed to emerge during the LM pre-training, motivating us to investigate how optimization, data distribution, loss function, and model architecture in LM pre-training influence its emergence. We highlight that attention sink emerges after effective optimization on sufficient training data. The sink position is highly correlated with the loss function and data distribution. Most importantly, we find that attention sink acts more like key biases, storing extra attention scores, which could be non-informative and not contribute to the value computation. We also observe that this phenomenon (at least partially) stems from tokens' inner dependence on attention scores as a result of softmax normalization.
